notes.front: What is basic empty weight?
notes.back: The standard empty weight plus the weight of any optional and special equipment installed.
notes.explanation: Standard empty weight already includes the airframe, engines, permanently installed equipment, unusable fuel and full engine oil, so basic empty weight is the aircraft as presently equipped.
notes.example: Like a car’s kerb weight with its fitted roof rack and tow bar included, but for an aircraft.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 10, “Terms and Definitions”, p. 10-4
notes.evidence: weight plus the weight of optional and special

notes.front: What is useful load?
notes.back: The basic empty weight subtracted from the maximum allowable gross weight: what the pilot may load.
notes.explanation: It is made up of the pilot, copilot, passengers, baggage, usable fuel and drainable oil, and the term applies to general aviation aircraft only.
notes.example: Like the payload rating of a van, but counting the driver and the fuel as well as the cargo.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 10, “Terms and Definitions”, p. 10-5
notes.evidence: It is the basic empty weight subtracted from the

notes.front: In weight and balance, what is the datum?
notes.back: An imaginary vertical plane or line, set by the manufacturer, from which all arm measurements are taken.
notes.explanation: Once the datum is chosen, all moment arms and the CG range are measured from it; its location is arbitrary and may differ between aircraft.
notes.example: Like the zero mark on a tape measure, but fixed to the airframe by its designer rather than at the nose.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 10, “Terms and Definitions”, p. 10-5
notes.evidence: Datum (reference datum)—an imaginary vertical

notes.front: In weight and balance, what is an arm?
notes.back: The horizontal distance in inches from the datum to the CG of an item.
notes.explanation: Its sign is plus when the item is aft of the datum and minus when it is forward of it.
notes.example: Like a child’s distance from the pivot of a seesaw, but measured from a fixed zero point on the aircraft.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 10, “Terms and Definitions”, p. 10-4
notes.evidence: from the reference datum line to the CG of an item.

notes.front: In weight and balance, what is a moment?
notes.back: The weight of an item multiplied by its arm, expressed in pound-inches (in-lb).
notes.explanation: A moment measures the tendency of a weight to rotate about a point; the total moment is the aircraft’s weight times the distance from the datum to its CG.
notes.example: Like the turning effect of a spanner, but taken about the datum: 150 lb at 40 in is 6,000 in-lb.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 10, “Terms and Definitions”, p. 10-5
notes.evidence: Moment—the product of the weight of an item

notes.front: What are center of gravity limits?
notes.back: The specified forward and aft points within which the CG must be located during flight.
notes.explanation: The manufacturer sets them, and the distance between the forward and aft limits is the CG range.
notes.example: Like the safe zone on a seesaw where the pivot can sit and the board still balances, but along the aircraft’s length.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 10, “Terms and Definitions”, p. 10-5
notes.evidence: CG limits—the specified forward and aft points within

notes.front: What is maximum ramp weight?
notes.back: The total weight of a loaded aircraft including all fuel; it exceeds takeoff weight by the fuel burned in taxi and run-up.
notes.explanation: Ramp weight may also be called taxi weight, because it is the weight before any fuel is used on the ground.
notes.example: Like a car’s weight as it leaves the driveway, before any petrol is used getting to the motorway.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 10, “Terms and Definitions”, p. 10-5
notes.evidence: aircraft including all fuel. It is greater than the takeoff

notes.front: What is pressure altitude?
notes.back: The height above the standard datum plane: the altitude shown when the altimeter is set to 29.92 "Hg.
notes.explanation: The standard datum plane is the level where pressure is 29.92 "Hg, and as pressure changes it may lie below, at or above sea level.
notes.example: Like measuring height from a floor that rises and falls with the weather, instead of from the sea.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 11, “Pressure Altitude”, p. 11-3
notes.evidence: Pressure altitude is the height above the standard datum

notes.front: What is the crosswind component of a wind?
notes.back: The part of the natural wind acting at 90° to the aircraft’s track.
notes.explanation: The greater the crosswind component, the harder it is to stop the aircraft weathervaning on the ground.
notes.example: Like a river current pushing a swimmer sideways, not the part that slows them down.
notes.source: FAA, Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 9, “Crosswind After-Landing Roll”, p. 9-18
notes.evidence: It has a headwind component acting along the airplane’s ground track and a crosswind component acting 90° to its track.

notes.front: What is the headwind component of a wind?
notes.back: The part of the natural wind acting along the aircraft’s ground track.
notes.explanation: For a given wind and runway, the handbook finds it, with the crosswind component, from a crosswind component chart.
notes.example: Like the breeze in a cyclist’s face on a straight road, ignoring any gust from the side.
notes.source: FAA, Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 9, “Crosswind After-Landing Roll”, p. 9-18
notes.evidence: the direction the air mass is traveling. It has a headwind component acting along the airplane’s ground track

notes.front: What is the best angle of climb speed (VX)?
notes.back: The speed giving the highest altitude in a given horizontal distance.
notes.explanation: Maximum angle of climb compares altitude gained with distance travelled, so VX is the speed for clearing obstacles close ahead.
notes.example: Like taking the steepest path up a bank to clear a wall at its foot, even though the climb is slow.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 11, “Performance Speeds”, p. 11-18
notes.evidence: VX—the speed at which the aircraft obtains the highest

notes.front: What is the best rate of climb speed (VY)?
notes.back: The speed giving the greatest increase in altitude per unit of time.
notes.explanation: Maximum rate of climb compares altitude gained with the time taken, so VY gets the aircraft highest soonest.
notes.example: Like the route up a hill that gets a walker highest in an hour, even if it covers more ground than the steepest path.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 11, “Performance Speeds”, p. 11-18
notes.evidence: VY—the speed at which the aircraft obtains the maximum

notes.front: What is an aircraft’s service ceiling?
notes.back: The altitude at which it can no longer climb faster than 100 feet per minute.
notes.explanation: Climb performance falls with altitude because power required rises while power available falls.
notes.example: Like the point on a long hill where an old car can only creep upward, though it has not quite stopped climbing.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 11, “Climb Performance Factors”, p. 11-8
notes.evidence: which the aircraft is unable to climb at a rate greater than 100

notes.front: What is an aircraft’s absolute ceiling?
notes.back: The altitude with no excess power, where the rate of climb is zero and only one speed holds level flight.
notes.explanation: As altitude increases, power required rises and power available falls until nothing is left over for climbing.
notes.example: Like a car at full throttle that can only just hold its speed on a slope, with nothing left to go faster.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 11, “Climb Performance Factors”, p. 11-8
notes.evidence: there is no excess of power and only one speed allows steady,

notes.front: What is the maximum demonstrated crosswind component?
notes.back: The crosswind in which the aircraft was shown to be landable during certification testing; it is published in the aircraft’s handbook.
notes.explanation: Certification requires landing in a 90° crosswind of up to two-tenths of the power-off stalling speed with gear and flaps down, flown by a pilot of average skill.
notes.example: Like a tested towing figure in a car’s manual: shown to work in testing, not a promise about anything stronger.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 11, “Crosswind and Headwind Component Chart”, p. 11-25
notes.evidence: component is published in the AFM/POH. The crosswind and

notes.front: What is best glide speed?
notes.back: The airspeed at which the aircraft glides furthest for the least altitude lost in non-powered flight.
notes.explanation: That is why a pilot who loses engine power establishes it and trims for it: it gives the most distance for the height available.
notes.example: Like a cyclist freewheeling downhill at the pace that carries them furthest without pedalling.
notes.source: FAA, Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Glossary, “Best glide”, p. G-3
notes.evidence: Best glide. The airspeed in which the aircraft glides the furthest for the least altitude lost when in non-powered flight.

notes.front: What is VS0?
notes.back: The stalling speed or minimum steady flight speed in the landing configuration.
notes.explanation: In small aircraft it is the power-off stall speed at maximum landing weight in the landing configuration, and it marks the bottom of the white arc.
notes.example: Like the slowest a cyclist can ride with the brakes dragging, but for an aircraft with flaps and gear down.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 8, “Airspeed Indicator Markings”, p. 8-9
notes.evidence: Lower limit of white arc (VS0)—the stalling speed
introduces: stalling speed in the landing configuration

notes.front: What is VS1?
notes.back: The stalling speed or minimum steady flight speed obtained in a specified configuration.
notes.explanation: For most aircraft it is the power-off stall speed at maximum takeoff weight in the clean configuration, and it marks the bottom of the green arc.
notes.example: Like VS0, but with the flaps and gear tidied away.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 8, “Airspeed Indicator Markings”, p. 8-9
notes.evidence: Lower limit of green arc (VS1)—the stalling speed
introduces: stalling speed in a specified configuration

notes.front: What is VFE?
notes.back: The highest speed permitted with the wing flaps in a prescribed extended position.
notes.explanation: The limit exists because of the air loads on the flap structure, and it marks the top of the white arc.
notes.example: Like a speed limit for driving with the boot lid open, set to protect the lid rather than the car.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 11, “Performance Speeds”, p. 11-18
notes.evidence: VFE—the highest speed permissible with the wing flaps in a

notes.front: What is VNO?
notes.back: The maximum structural cruising speed: the maximum speed for normal operation.
notes.explanation: Above it, exceeding the limit load factor may permanently deform the structure, so the handbook says not to exceed it except in smooth air.
notes.example: Like a road’s everyday speed limit that you may pass only on a perfectly smooth stretch.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 11, “Performance Speeds”, p. 11-19
notes.evidence: VN0—the maximum speed for normal operation or the

notes.front: What is VNE?
notes.back: The never-exceed speed, shown by the red line on the airspeed indicator.
notes.explanation: Operating above it is prohibited because it may result in damage or structural failure.
notes.example: Like the red line on a car’s rev counter, but for airspeed.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 8, “Airspeed Indicator Markings”, p. 8-9
notes.evidence: Red line (VNE)—never exceed speed. Operating above

notes.front: What two harms does operating above the maximum weight limitation cause?
notes.back: It compromises the aircraft’s structural integrity and adversely affects its performance.
notes.explanation: The handbook opens its weight and balance chapter with this, calling compliance with the limits critical to flight safety.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 10, “Introduction”, p. 10-1
notes.evidence: Operating above the maximum weight limitation compromises the structural integrity of an aircraft and adversely affects its performance.

notes.front: Operation with the CG outside the approved limits results in {{c1::control difficulty}}.
notes.back: control difficulty
notes.explanation: Weight limits protect the structure and performance, while CG limits protect the pilot’s ability to control the aircraft.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 10, “Introduction”, p. 10-1
notes.evidence: Operation with the center of gravity (CG) outside the approved limits results in control difficulty.

notes.front: An overloaded aircraft needs a {{c1::higher}} takeoff speed.
notes.back: higher
notes.explanation: A heavier aircraft needs more lift to leave the ground, and the handbook lists a higher takeoff speed first among overload deficiencies.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 10, “Effects of Weight”, p. 10-2
notes.evidence: •    Higher takeoff speed

notes.front: An overloaded aircraft has a {{c1::longer}} takeoff run.
notes.back: longer
notes.explanation: It must reach a higher speed with more mass to accelerate, so the ground run grows.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 10, “Effects of Weight”, p. 10-2
notes.evidence: •    Longer takeoff run

notes.front: Excess weight {{c1::reduces}} both the rate and the angle of climb.
notes.back: reduces
notes.explanation: Extra weight leaves less excess thrust and power for climbing, so the handbook lists a reduced rate and angle of climb among the deficiencies of an overloaded aircraft.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 10, “Effects of Weight”, p. 10-2
notes.evidence: Reduced rate and angle of climb

notes.front: An overloaded aircraft has a {{c1::lower}} maximum altitude.
notes.back: lower
notes.explanation: The handbook lists a lower maximum altitude among the most important deficiencies of an overloaded aircraft.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 10, “Effects of Weight”, p. 10-2
notes.evidence: •    Lower maximum altitude

notes.front: An overloaded aircraft has a {{c1::shorter}} range.
notes.back: shorter
notes.explanation: Excessive weight reduces flight performance in almost every respect, so the handbook lists shorter range among the most important deficiencies of an overloaded aircraft.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 10, “Effects of Weight”, p. 10-2
notes.evidence: deficiencies of an overloaded aircraft are:

notes.front: An overloaded aircraft has a {{c1::reduced}} cruising speed.
notes.back: reduced
notes.explanation: Reduced cruising speed is one of the handbook’s listed overload deficiencies.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 10, “Effects of Weight”, p. 10-2
notes.evidence: •    Reduced cruising speed

notes.front: An overloaded aircraft has {{c1::reduced}} manoeuvrability.
notes.back: reduced
notes.explanation: Reduced maneuverability, in the handbook’s spelling, is one of its listed overload deficiencies.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 10, “Effects of Weight”, p. 10-2
notes.evidence: Excessive weight reduces the flight performance in almost

notes.front: An overloaded aircraft has a {{c1::higher}} stalling speed.
notes.back: higher
notes.explanation: A higher stalling speed is one of the handbook’s listed overload deficiencies.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 10, “Effects of Weight”, p. 10-2
notes.evidence: •    Higher stalling speed

notes.front: An overloaded aircraft needs a {{c1::higher}} approach and landing speed.
notes.back: higher
notes.explanation: A heavier aircraft needs more speed to support its weight at the landing angle of attack.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 10, “Effects of Weight”, p. 10-2
notes.evidence: Higher approach and landing speed

notes.front: An overloaded aircraft has a {{c1::longer}} landing roll.
notes.back: longer
notes.explanation: It must touch down faster, and minimum landing distance varies in direct proportion to gross weight.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 10, “Effects of Weight”, p. 10-2
notes.evidence: •    Longer landing roll

notes.front: Besides speeds and distances, what does overloading do to the aircraft’s nose wheel or tail wheel?
notes.back: It puts excessive weight on it.
notes.explanation: The handbook ends its list of overload deficiencies with excessive weight on the nose wheel or tail wheel.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 10, “Effects of Weight”, p. 10-2
notes.evidence: Excessive weight on the nose wheel or tail wheel

notes.front: Aviation gasoline weighs about {{c1::6 pounds}} per gallon.
notes.back: 6 pounds
notes.explanation: At that weight, thirty gallons of fuel may weigh more than one passenger.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 10, “Weight Changes”, p. 10-2
notes.evidence: weight—6 pounds per gallon. Thirty gallons of fuel may

notes.front: You top up with 35 gallons of aviation gasoline. How much weight have you added?
notes.explanation: Aviation gasoline is taken as 6 lb per gallon, so fuel alone can equal a passenger’s weight.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 10, “Weight Changes”, p. 10-2
notes.evidence: simply altering the fuel load. Gasoline has considerable

notes.front: With full fuel and a new passenger aboard, your aircraft is 60 lb over maximum weight. What does the handbook suggest?
notes.back: B) Take less fuel, and allow for the shorter range in planning
notes.choices:
A) Leave the fuel and baggage as they are
B) Take less fuel, and allow for the shorter range in planning
C) Load full fuel and move the passenger to the back
notes.choicesExplained: A leaves the aircraft overweight. C does not reduce weight at all; moving a passenger changes balance, not total weight.
notes.explanation: Reducing fuel lowers weight quickly, but the resulting loss of range must be taken into account in flight planning.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 10, “Weight Changes”, p. 10-2
notes.evidence: weight by reducing fuel, the resulting decrease in the range

notes.front: How does tail-heavy loading affect stability and stall or spin recovery?
notes.back: It seriously affects longitudinal stability and reduces the ability to recover from stalls and spins.
notes.explanation: Tail-heavy loading also produces very light control forces, which make it easy to overstress the aircraft.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 10, “Stability”, p. 10-3
notes.evidence: effect upon longitudinal stability, and reduces the capability

notes.front: Your loading sums show the CG just behind the aft limit, with the total weight well under maximum. What is the handbook’s logical fix?
notes.back: A) Seat the heavier passengers in the front seats
notes.choices:
A) Seat the heavier passengers in the front seats
B) Put the heaviest bags in the aft baggage area
C) Add fuel to bring the weight up
notes.choicesExplained: B moves the CG further aft. C adds weight without fixing the aft CG, and fuel in wing tanks near the CG has little effect on it.
notes.explanation: The pilot controls CG through the placement of baggage, cargo and passengers, so a tail-heavy aircraft calls for heavy passengers forward.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 10, “Control”, p. 10-3
notes.evidence: it is only logical to place heavy passengers in forward seats.

notes.front: A pilot flies with the CG at the extreme aft end of the range after loading heavy bags behind the rear seats. What should they expect?
notes.back: B) Very light control forces and poorer stall recovery
notes.choices:
A) Heavy control forces and difficulty raising the nose
B) Very light control forces and poorer stall recovery
C) No change, as long as the weight is legal
notes.choicesExplained: A describes a forward CG. C is wrong: balance affects stability and control whatever the weight.
notes.explanation: An aft CG reduces longitudinal stability and gives light control forces, making it easy to overstress the aircraft.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 10, “Control”, p. 10-3
notes.evidence: violent stall characteristics, and very light control forces

notes.front: Must a Part 91 pilot do a weight and balance calculation before every flight?
notes.back: There is no specific requirement, but section 91.9 requires complying with the approved operating limits, which include weight and balance.
notes.explanation: Charts and graphs in the approved flight manual let the pilot make these computations.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 10, “Management of Weight and Balance Control”, p. 10-4
notes.evidence: under 14 CFR part 91 to conduct weight and balance
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Can an aircraft be out of CG limits without exceeding its useful load?
notes.back: Yes; and aircraft that are hard to load out of CG limits can still be overloaded.
notes.explanation: So the total weight and the CG location must both be checked.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 10, “Weight and Balance Restrictions”, p. 10-7
notes.evidence: be out of CG limits even though the useful load has not been

notes.front: An aircraft’s maximum allowable gross weight is 2,550 lb and its basic empty weight is 1,640 lb. What is its useful load?
notes.explanation: Useful load is the basic empty weight subtracted from the maximum allowable gross weight, and it must cover occupants, baggage, usable fuel and drainable oil.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 10, “Terms and Definitions”, p. 10-5

notes.back: full engine oil

notes.front: An aircraft is certified for 2,550 lb. Can it safely take off at 2,550 lb from a high, hot, humid airfield?
notes.back: B) Not necessarily: high density altitude may call for a weight reduction
notes.choices:
A) Yes: certification at that weight covers all conditions
B) Not necessarily: high density altitude may call for a weight reduction
C) Only if the runway is grass
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the handbook says certification at a weight does not mean it can take off safely at that weight in all conditions. C is too narrow: elevation, heat and humidity matter on any surface.
notes.explanation: Conditions that raise density altitude hurt takeoff and climb performance, and may require less weight before flight is attempted.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 10, “Weight and Balance Restrictions”, p. 10-6

notes.front: Weight × {{c1::arm}} = moment.
notes.back: arm
notes.explanation: The moment is the product of an item’s weight and its distance from the datum.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 10, “Principles of Weight and Balance Computations”, p. 10-6
notes.evidence: distance from the datum (arm), the product is the moment.

notes.front: How do you find the CG from a completed loading table?
notes.back: Divide the total moment by the total weight.
notes.explanation: The result is the CG’s distance from the datum, which is then compared with the CG range.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 10, “Computational Method”, p. 10-7

notes.explanation: List each weight and moment, total both, then divide the total moment by the total weight.

notes.back: A) Yes: within both weight and CG limits

A) Yes: within both weight and CG limits
B) No: over maximum weight

notes.back: Between 82.1 and 84.7 inches aft of the datum.

notes.front: When weight is shifted forward in the aircraft, what happens to total weight and total moment?
notes.back: Total weight is unchanged; total moment decreases.
notes.explanation: Moving weight aft increases total moments, and the change is proportional to the weight moved.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 10, “Weight Shifting”, p. 10-10
notes.evidence: moved forward, the total moments decrease; when weight

notes.front: A 2,400 lb aircraft has its CG at 45.0 in. You move 60 lb of bags from station 100 to station 40. New CG?
notes.back: 43.5 in: the CG moves 1.5 in forward (60 × 60 ÷ 2,400).
notes.explanation: When the CG shifts forward, the change is subtracted from the old CG; when it shifts aft, it is added.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 10, “Weight Addition or Removal”, p. 10-11
notes.evidence: forward, the rCG is subtracted from the old CG.

notes.front: How can you read pressure altitude directly in the aircraft?
notes.back: Set the altimeter’s barometric scale to 29.92 "Hg and read the indicated altitude.
notes.explanation: The other methods are correcting field elevation for the reported altimeter setting, or using a flight computer.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 11, “Pressure Altitude”, p. 11-3
notes.evidence: By setting the barometric scale of the altimeter to

notes.front: Field elevation is 1,200 ft and the altimeter setting is 29.72 "Hg. About what is the pressure altitude?
notes.back: About 1,400 ft.
notes.explanation: The setting is 0.20 "Hg below standard, and pressure falls about 1 "Hg per 1,000 ft, so add about 200 ft.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 11, “Atmospheric Pressure”, p. 11-2
notes.evidence: at a rate of approximately 1 "Hg per 1,000 feet of altitude gain

notes.front: An airport sits at 3,000 ft and the altimeter setting is 30.12 "Hg. About what is the pressure altitude?
notes.back: A) About 2,800 ft
notes.choices:
A) About 2,800 ft
B) About 3,200 ft
C) 3,000 ft exactly
notes.choicesExplained: B applies the correction the wrong way: a setting above 29.92 means subtracting. C ignores the non-standard pressure.
notes.explanation: The setting is 0.20 "Hg above standard, worth about 200 ft at roughly 1 "Hg per 1,000 ft, so pressure altitude is below field elevation.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 11, “Atmospheric Pressure”, p. 11-2
notes.evidence: at a rate of approximately 1 "Hg per 1,000 feet of altitude gain

notes.front: Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for {{c1::nonstandard temperature}}.
notes.back: nonstandard temperature
notes.explanation: So density altitude is found by first finding pressure altitude, then correcting it for temperature.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 11, “Density Altitude”, p. 11-3
notes.evidence: Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard

notes.front: What are two conditions that result in a high density altitude?
notes.back: Any two of: high elevation, low atmospheric pressure, high temperature, high humidity.
notes.explanation: Each makes the air thinner, and they are often combined.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 11, “Density Altitude”, p. 11-4
notes.evidence: result in a high density altitude are high elevations, low

notes.front: At your airfield the pressure altitude is 2,000 ft and the temperature is well above standard. How does the density altitude compare with the pressure altitude?
notes.back: A) Higher than the pressure altitude
notes.choices:
A) Higher than the pressure altitude
B) Lower than the pressure altitude
C) The same as the pressure altitude
notes.choicesExplained: B would need colder than standard air. C holds only at standard temperature.
notes.explanation: Density altitude is computed from pressure altitude and temperature, and warm air is less dense.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 11, “Density Altitude”, p. 11-4
notes.evidence: Density altitude is computed using pressure altitude and

notes.front: As the water content of the air increases, what happens to density altitude and performance?
notes.back: The air becomes less dense, so density altitude rises and performance falls.
notes.explanation: Water vapour is lighter than air, so moist air is lighter than dry air.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 11, “Effects of Humidity (Moisture) on Density”, p. 11-5
notes.evidence: water content of the air increases, the air becomes less dense,

notes.front: Two fields have the same elevation, pressure and temperature. One is muggy after rain; the other is dry. At which should you expect the poorer takeoff performance?
notes.back: A) The humid field
notes.choices:
A) The humid field
B) The dry field
C) Neither: humidity has no effect
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: dry air is denser. C is wrong: humidity is not charted, but it still lowers performance.
notes.explanation: Moist air is less dense, which raises density altitude.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 11, “Effects of Humidity (Moisture) on Density”, p. 11-5
notes.evidence: consideration. Expect a decrease in overall performance in

notes.front: What three effects does increased gross weight have on takeoff?
notes.back: Higher lift-off speed, greater mass to accelerate, and more retarding force (drag and ground friction).
notes.explanation: Each of the three lengthens the takeoff, which is why weight is so important in predicting takeoff distance.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 11, “Takeoff Performance”, p. 11-15
notes.evidence: gross weight can be considered to produce a threefold effect

notes.front: A headwind of 10 percent of the takeoff airspeed reduces takeoff distance by about {{c1::19}} percent.
notes.explanation: A headwind lets the aircraft reach lift-off speed at a lower groundspeed.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 11, “Takeoff Performance”, p. 11-15
notes.evidence: A headwind that is 10 percent of the takeoff airspeed reduces

notes.front: A tailwind of 10 percent of the takeoff airspeed increases takeoff distance by about {{c1::21}} percent.
notes.explanation: A tailwind makes the aircraft reach a greater groundspeed before it attains lift-off airspeed.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 11, “Takeoff Performance”, p. 11-15
notes.evidence: tailwind that is 10 percent of the takeoff airspeed increases

notes.front: The wind is 280° at 12 knots and your takeoff will be tight. Runways 10 and 28 are the same length. Which gives the shorter takeoff?
notes.back: A) Runway 28
notes.choices:
A) Runway 28
B) Runway 10
C) Either: wind does not change takeoff distance
notes.choicesExplained: B gives a 12-knot tailwind, lengthening the run. C is wrong: the handbook calls the effect of wind on takeoff distance large.
notes.explanation: Taking off into the wind lets the aircraft reach lift-off speed at a lower groundspeed.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 11, “Takeoff Performance”, p. 11-15

notes.front: A 10 percent excess landing speed causes at least a {{c1::21}} percent increase in landing distance.
notes.explanation: The extra speed adds kinetic energy for the brakes to absorb and extra lift that reduces the load on the braking wheels.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 11, “Landing Performance”, p. 11-17
notes.evidence: A ten percent excess landing speed causes at least a 21

notes.front: What runway surface do performance charts typically assume?
notes.back: Paved, level, smooth and dry.
notes.explanation: No two runways are alike, so the surface and slope at the actual airport must be allowed for.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 11, “Runway Surface and Gradient”, p. 11-12
notes.evidence: Typically, performance chart information assumes paved,

notes.front: An upsloping runway gives a {{c1::longer}} takeoff ground run but typically a shorter landing roll.
notes.back: longer
notes.explanation: An upslope impedes acceleration; a downslope aids it on takeoff but lengthens the landing.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 11, “Runway Surface and Gradient”, p. 11-13
notes.evidence: acceleration and results in a longer ground run during takeoff.

notes.front: A short farm strip slopes noticeably and the wind is calm. To keep the landing roll short, which way should you land?
notes.back: A) Land uphill
notes.choices:
A) Land uphill
B) Land downhill
C) It makes no difference
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: landing on a downslope increases landing distance. C ignores the gradient.
notes.explanation: Landing on an upsloping runway typically reduces the landing roll.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 11, “Runway Surface and Gradient”, p. 11-13
notes.evidence: However, landing on an upsloping runway typically reduces

notes.front: Performance chart data come from test flights in what sort of aircraft and with what piloting?
notes.back: A new aircraft in good working order, flown with average piloting skills.
notes.explanation: So the numbers will not be accurate for an aircraft in poor condition or in adverse conditions, and must then be adjusted.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 11, “Performance Charts”, p. 11-19
notes.evidence: under normal operating conditions while using average

notes.front: A takeoff table gives 1,400 ft over a 50 ft obstacle. Its note says decrease distances 10% for each 8 knots of headwind. With 16 knots of headwind?
notes.back: 1,120 ft (a 20% reduction).
notes.explanation: Every chart states its conditions and has notes on adapting the figures to actual conditions.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 11, “Performance Charts”, p. 11-19
notes.evidence: Every chart is based on certain conditions and contains

notes.front: On a combined landing distance graph, in what order are the factors usually entered?
notes.back: A) Temperature, pressure altitude, weight, wind, obstacle height
notes.choices:
A) Temperature, pressure altitude, weight, wind, obstacle height
B) Weight only
C) Wind, then temperature, then weight, then pressure altitude
notes.choicesExplained: B ignores the other conditions the graph compensates for. C is out of order: you start from the temperature scale and pressure altitude line.
notes.explanation: The handbook works across the graph from outside air temperature to pressure altitude, then through the weight, wind and obstacle reference lines.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 11, “Landing Charts”, p. 11-27
notes.evidence: a combined landing distance graph and allows compensation

notes.front: A climb chart reads 1 gal, 2 min, 3 NM at your 2,000 ft field and 4 gal, 11 min, 17 NM at 8,000 ft. Fuel, time and distance to climb?
notes.back: 3 gal, 9 min, 14 NM.
notes.explanation: Subtract each departure figure from the matching cruise figure.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 11, “Climb and Cruise Charts”, p. 11-23
notes.evidence: Take each set of numbers for fuel, time, and distance

notes.front: A cruise and range performance table gives endurance and range. What two other values does it give?
notes.back: True airspeed and fuel consumption.
notes.explanation: The values are for specific cruise configurations of altitude and power setting.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 11, “Climb and Cruise Charts”, p. 11-24
notes.evidence: This type of table is designed to give TAS, fuel consumption,

notes.front: A cruise table shows 8 gallons per hour at your chosen power, and you have 40 gallons usable. What endurance does that give, with no reserve?
notes.back: 5 hours.
notes.explanation: Endurance is the usable fuel divided by the fuel flow at that power setting.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 11, “Climb and Cruise Charts”, p. 11-24
notes.evidence: endurance in hours, and range in miles at specific cruise

notes.front: Landing on runway 09 with the wind 120° at 20 knots, what do the crosswind and headwind components come to?
notes.back: About 10 knots crosswind and 17 knots headwind (30° wind angle).
notes.explanation: Find the angle between wind and runway, then follow it to the wind speed and read both components off the chart.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 11, “Crosswind and Headwind Component Chart”, p. 11-25
notes.evidence: headwind component chart allows for figuring the headwind

notes.front: Runway 36, wind 270° at 12 knots. What are the components?
notes.back: A) 12 knots crosswind, no headwind
notes.choices:
A) 12 knots crosswind, no headwind
B) 6 knots crosswind, 6 knots headwind
C) No crosswind, 12 knots headwind
notes.choicesExplained: B splits the wind as if it were at 45°. C treats a wind straight across as a headwind.
notes.explanation: A wind at 90° to the runway acts wholly across the track, so all of it is crosswind.
notes.source: FAA, Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 9, “Crosswind After-Landing Roll”, p. 9-18
notes.evidence: acting 90° to its track. The other factor is the wind induced by the forward movement of the airplane

notes.front: An aircraft’s power-off stall speed with gear and flaps down is 50 knots. What 90° crosswind must certification show it can land in?
notes.back: 10 knots (two-tenths of 50).
notes.explanation: Certification tests landing in 90° crosswinds up to 0.2 times that stall speed; the result is published as the maximum demonstrated crosswind component.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 11, “Crosswind and Headwind Component Chart”, p. 11-25
notes.evidence: of the aircraft’s stalling speed with power off, gear down,

notes.front: You are departing a short strip with tall trees just past its end. Which speed should you climb at until they are cleared?
notes.back: A) VX
notes.choices:
A) VX
B) VY
C) Best glide speed
notes.choicesExplained: B gives more height per minute but less per foot of ground. C is for gliding without power, not climbing.
notes.explanation: VX gives the most altitude for the least horizontal distance, which is what an obstacle close ahead demands.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 11, “Climb Performance”, p. 11-7
notes.evidence: AOC is when taking off from a short airfield surrounded by

notes.front: With no obstacles ahead, you want to reach your cruising altitude as quickly as possible. Which speed?
notes.back: A) VY
notes.choices:
A) VY
B) VX
C) VNE
notes.choicesExplained: B gains more height per mile but less per minute. C is a structural limit, not a climb speed.
notes.explanation: VY gives the greatest altitude gain per unit of time, so it expedites a climb to altitude.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 11, “Climb Performance”, p. 11-7
notes.evidence: Maximum ROC expedites a climb to an assigned altitude.

notes.front: Besides more weight, what are two things that reduce both maximum angle and maximum rate of climb?
notes.back: Any two of: higher altitude, landing gear down, flaps down.
notes.explanation: Each of them decreases both the excess thrust and the excess power that climbing depends on.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 11, “Climb Performance Factors”, p. 11-8
notes.evidence: decrease both excess thrust and excess power for all aircraft.

notes.front: Where do the speeds for maximum rate and maximum angle of climb converge?
notes.back: At the absolute ceiling.
notes.explanation: There no excess power is left, and only one speed allows steady, level flight.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 11, “Climb Performance Factors”, p. 11-8
notes.evidence: altitude is increased, these various speeds finally converge

notes.front: Your engine quits in cruise, well above best glide speed. What should you do with the airspeed first?
notes.back: A) Let the aircraft slow to best glide speed, then lower the nose and trim
notes.choices:
A) Let the aircraft slow to best glide speed, then lower the nose and trim
B) Dive at once to gain speed
C) Hold the cruise speed
notes.choicesExplained: B throws away height. C trades height for speed you do not need.
notes.explanation: Above best glide speed the pilot lets the aircraft slow, even climbing to bleed off speed, before trimming for best glide.
notes.source: FAA, Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 9, “Emergency Approaches and Landings (Simulated)”, p. 9-28
notes.evidence: If the simulated power failure occurs while above best glide speed, the pilot allows the airplane to slow

notes.front: If power fails at or below best glide speed, what should the pilot do?
notes.back: Lower the nose immediately to keep or regain best glide speed.
notes.explanation: Below best glide speed, lowering the nose both increases the airspeed and shallows the descent angle.
notes.source: FAA, Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 9, “Emergency Approaches and Landings (Simulated)”, p. 9-28
notes.evidence: If the failure occurs at or below best glide speed, the nose should be lowered immediately

notes.front: In a power-off approach into a headwind, what airspeed adjustment does the handbook allow to reach the aiming point?
notes.back: Flying slightly above best glide speed.
notes.explanation: Wind changes gliding distance over the ground, and the pilot corrects for it with pitch, not by stretching the glide.
notes.source: FAA, Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 9, “Power-Off Accuracy Approaches”, p. 9-25
notes.evidence: or increase airspeed slightly above best glide in a headwind

notes.front: How do VX and VY differ in what they maximise?
notes.back: VX: most altitude for horizontal distance covered. VY: most altitude for time taken.
notes.explanation: VX suits obstacle clearance near the runway; VY suits getting to cruising altitude quickly.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 11, “Climb Performance”, p. 11-7
notes.evidence: AOC is a comparison of altitude gained relative to distance

notes.front: How do the handling effects of a CG too far forward differ from those of a CG too far aft?
notes.back: Forward: nose-heavy, hard to flare, higher stall speed. Aft: less stable, very light control forces, violent stalls.
notes.explanation: A forward CG costs elevator authority; an aft CG costs stability and makes overstressing easy.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 10, “Control”, p. 10-3
